overlap_rationale: Both Study A (IJURR 2008) and Study B (Geoforum 2008, cited as forthcoming in Study A) are companion qualitative-historical case studies by Michelle Kooy and Karen Bakker derived from the exact same SSHRC-funded research project on colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta's water supply infrastructure. Both articles draw on the same 2003 Dutch colonial archival research in Amsterdam, Leiden and Den Haag and the same 2004–2006 Jakarta fieldwork (interviews with water supply professionals, participant observation with local and international NGOs, and policy/media document analysis) conducted with the same research assistants (Endah Shofiani and E.J. Martijn). While Study A frames the material around Foucauldian technologies of government, hygiene discourses and urban subjectivities and Study B critiques Graham and Marvin's 'splintering urbanism' thesis across four infrastructure periods, they analyze the same underlying archival corpus, fieldwork interviews, historical statistics (e.g., identical 1929/1930 Eggink kampung vs. European connection figures and contemporary 40,000 illegal connection estimates) and case setting.
study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative-historical genealogy of urban water supply in colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta, Indonesia (1870s–2006), based on 2003 colonial archival research in the Netherlands (Nationaal Archief in Den Haag, KITLV in Leiden, KIT in Amsterdam) and 2004–2006 Jakarta fieldwork comprising interviews with local and international water supply professionals, participant observation with NGOs in urban poor communities (kampungs), and discourse analysis of media, donor and utility documents (no numeric respondent N reported).
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative-historical case study of urban water supply fragmentation in colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta, Indonesia (1870–2007), drawing on the same Dutch colonial archival records (Amsterdam and Leiden), PAM Jaya/KIP/World Bank/JICA utility and policy reports, and Jakarta fieldwork interviews with water supply professionals and local/international NGO staff assisted by Endah Shofiani and E.J. Martijn (no numeric respondent N reported).
